_comment: Cross-language contract for barcode nomenclatures (BOF-043, BAN-488).
The parser lives once, in packages/domain/src/barcode, and both the register and the
back-office rule tester call it. What has never been asserted is the join: that a rule an
operator authors in the back office reaches the till in a shape that parser understands.
So `rules` below is what the back office must ship — BarcodeNomenclatureTest authors these
through the real endpoint and asserts the bootstrap payload matches, field for field — and
`cases` is what the parser must then make of them, asserted by
Either side drifting fails one of the two. Changing the expectations here is a deliberate
act that fails both until both are updated, which is the point.
Every `scan` carries a real EAN-13 check digit. The pattern match does not verify one — it
recomputes the base code's — so an invalid barcode would parse identically and the fixture
would be describing something no printer produces.

rules._comment: Sequence 5, so it is tried first. Its pattern matches the weight rule's codes too — only the encoding gate keeps it from swallowing them, which is what makes the gate testable at all.
rules.name: Étiquette courte

cases.why: A weighed item: prefix 21, five digits of product code, then 2 integer and 3 decimal digits of weight. 01500 is 1.5 kg.
The same rule with a whole number of kilograms, which is where a naive decimal shift shows up as 2000 rather than 2.
A price-embedded label. Same shape, different meaning — and the field is 2 integer digits then 3 decimals, so 4.50 is written 04500, not 00450.
An alias rule reports the code it aliases to, not the code that was scanned.
An ordinary EAN-13 matches no rule and is still a perfectly good product lookup — the common case, and the one a too-greedy pattern would break.

The weight rule still wins on a 13-digit code even though an earlier rule's pattern also matches it — that rule is declared for EAN-8, and the encoding gate refuses it before the pattern is tried. Without the gate the scan would alias instead of weighing, and a weighed item would ring up as a badge.
The same earlier rule does fire on an 8-digit code, which is what it is for.
